How is Delaware organized, and who handles what when you sell a house?

Delaware has three counties, the fewest of any state: New Castle in the north, Kent in the middle and Sussex in the south. Each county seat is a different city. Wilmington serves New Castle, Dover serves Kent and Georgetown serves Sussex.

County governments do a lot of the work that touches a sale. Per Wikipedia's county list, New Castle and Sussex elect a County Council and Kent elects a Levy Court. These bodies handle zoning, sewer service, building codes and taxes.

Your first calls usually go to these county offices:

  • The Recorder of Deeds, who records your deed and collects transfer tax and recording fees.
  • The county assessment or tax office, which issues the bill and handles appeals.
  • The Register of Wills, if the owner has died.

We buy houses in Delaware and have local pages for Wilmington, Dover, Newark and Middletown. Those cities sit in New Castle and Kent counties, so the county rules below apply to them.

What does selling as-is for cash mean in Delaware?

It means the buyer takes the house in its current condition and you skip the repair list, the staging and the wait for a buyer's mortgage. It does not remove your disclosure duties.

Under the state's Buyer Property Protection Act, a seller of a one to four family home must disclose known material defects in writing, before signing a listing agreement, and update the disclosure if something changes before settlement. The seller also gives the buyer a Property Condition Report before an offer is made, and that form becomes part of the purchase agreement. Radon gets its own notice: sellers pass along any test results they hold and any known radon hazard.

Some transfers are exempt from those disclosure rules. The statute lists these, among others:

  • Transfers by a fiduciary while administering an estate, guardianship or trust.
  • Transfers under a court order.
  • Sheriff's sales and deeds in lieu of foreclosure.
  • Transfers to a spouse or to a lineal relative.

Even when you are exempt, a clear list of what you know about the house keeps the closing smooth.

What taxes and fees does a Delaware seller face at closing?

The main closing cost is the realty transfer tax. Title 30, Chapter 54 sets it at 3 percent of the property's value, or 2.5 percent where the county or municipality has enacted the full 1.5 percent local share. The law splits the tax equally between grantor and grantee, and absent a different agreement the burden falls on the grantor.

ItemWhat the Delaware Code says
Transfer tax rate3 percent, or 2.5 percent where the full local 1.5 percent applies
Who paysSplit equally between grantor and grantee, unless the parties agree otherwise
First-time buyer reductionGrantee's share reduced by 0.5 percent of the lesser of value or $400,000
Recording surcharges$5 Housing Development Fund and $25 Cultural Access Fund per document
Recorder fee schedulesSet by ordinance in each county

Several transfers are not taxed. These include conveyances between spouses, between parent and child, between siblings and between grandparent and grandchild. A conveyance to a lender in default, by sheriff's sale or in lieu of foreclosure, is also excluded.

The value used for the tax is the actual consideration. If the price is below the highest appraised value for local property tax, the appraised value is used unless the parties show a lower fair market value. An arm's length sale between unrelated parties is enough to show fair market value.

For a plain-language walk through, see our guide to recording a deed in Delaware.

What does the recorder require before a Delaware deed is accepted?

Each county has its own elected recorder, and a deed is not accepted until it meets a short list of conditions in Title 9, Chapter 96.

  • An affidavit of residence and gain, unless the transfer is one of the tax-exempt types.
  • The words "prepared by" and the drafter's name and address on the first page.
  • The county tax parcel number in a conspicuous place.
  • Proof the realty transfer tax was paid.
  • For a nonresident individual, pass-through entity or corporation, the tax return and any estimated income tax due.

In Kent County, the recorder will not take a deed until state and municipal transfer tax is paid, with the City of Dover tax carved out. Recording fees in New Castle and Sussex are set by ordinance, and Kent's are too. Ask the county office for the current schedule rather than relying on an old number.

How does foreclosure work in Delaware?

Delaware uses a judicial process. The lender sues out a writ of scire facias on the mortgage in the Superior Court of the county where the house sits, so a sheriff's sale follows a court case, not a private notice.

For an owner-occupied one to four family primary residence, the lender cannot file until 45 days after sending a notice of intent to foreclose by certified and first-class mail. The notice must carry a heading in English and Spanish urging the owner to act. The law also creates an Automatic Residential Mortgage Foreclosure Mediation Program for these homes. The complaint must come with a mediation notice that points the owner to the Attorney General's foreclosure hotline at 1-800-220-5424.

Once a property sells at a sheriff's sale, the buyer takes it free of the mortgagor's equity of redemption and later claims made by the mortgagor. That is why timing matters. A sale to a private buyer before the auction date can end the case and protect your credit in a way the auction cannot.

Our page on Delaware sheriff sales covers the sale steps. If you have received any court papers, read them for the mediation notice and respond before the dates listed.

How do you sell an inherited house in Delaware?

Start with the Register of Wills in the county where the person lived. State law requires the will to be filed there.

Sussex County's Register of Wills describes the steps this way:

  • Bring the original will and a certified death certificate, then call to schedule an appointment.
  • If the will is not self-proven, the witnesses or other qualified people take an oath at the office.
  • The office issues short certificates that let the personal representative act for the estate.
  • An inventory, including real estate, is due within three months of the letters being granted.
  • An accounting is due within one year. If the house sold, the settlement sheet is attached to it.

Kent County's Levy Court says the Register of Wills handles appointments, issues letters and closes the estate. Confirm details with your own county's office before you list.

The disclosure statute exempts transfers made by a fiduciary in administering an estate, which can simplify paperwork. Transfers between a parent and child carry no transfer tax, but a sale to an outside buyer does. Read our guide to Delaware estate and inheritance tax before you set a closing date.

What happens if the house has tenants?

Delaware's Residential Landlord-Tenant Code governs the lease whether it is written or oral. It says a written lease longer than one year is effective for only one year, and a lease with no stated term runs month to month.

Notice periods are long. A landlord ending a fixed-term lease needs to give at least 60 days' written notice before it expires. For a month-to-month tenancy, either side gives at least 60 days' notice, counted from the first day of the month after notice is received. If neither side acts, a lease of a year or more rolls into month-to-month.

Whether a sale cuts a lease short depends on the lease and on how the buyer takes title, so check with an attorney before promising a tenant any move-out date. Our pages on Delaware landlord tenant law and squatters rights and adverse possession go further. A house with people living in it can still be sold as-is, and you can tell us about the occupants up front.

How do property taxes and flood risk affect a Delaware sale?

Each county runs its own assessment process under Title 9, Chapter 83. If you think the assessed value is wrong, the timing differs by county:

  • New Castle: written notice of appeal must be filed with the Board of Assessment Review before March 15.
  • Kent and Sussex: the boards hear appeals from March 1 to May 31, or until all appeals are heard in a reassessment year.

An aggrieved appellant has 30 days from the postmark of the decision notice to go to Superior Court. If an appeal lowers the value and you overpaid by $50 or more, you are owed a refund. Our Delaware property tax guide covers exemptions and selling with tax due.

On flooding, the state's environmental agency, DNREC, says Delaware is highly vulnerable because of its low, flat land. It reports that sea levels along the coast are rising at roughly twice the global average and that heavier rain is raising inland flood risk too. It adds that many properties outside mapped floodplains are also at risk. If your house has water history, say so on the disclosure form and ask the county floodplain office about mapped zones.

Frequently asked questions

How many counties does Delaware have?

Three: New Castle, Kent and Sussex. Delaware has the fewest counties of any state, and each county has its own Recorder of Deeds, Register of Wills and tax office.

Who pays the transfer tax when I sell?

The rate is 3 percent, or 2.5 percent where the full local share applies, split equally between grantor and grantee. If the parties do not agree otherwise, the grantor bears the burden.

Is foreclosure judicial in Delaware?

Yes. The lender files a writ of scire facias in Superior Court. For owner-occupied homes of one to four units, a 45 day notice of intent comes first, and mediation is available.

Do I have to disclose problems when I sell as-is?

For most one to four family sales, yes. Known material defects and radon information go in writing. Fiduciary estate sales, sheriff's sales and some family transfers are exempt.

Where do I start if I inherited a house?

Call the Register of Wills in the county where the owner lived. Bring the original will and a certified death certificate and ask about an appointment.

How much notice does a Delaware tenant get?

A month-to-month tenancy needs at least 60 days' written notice from either side. A fixed-term lease needs at least 60 days' notice before its expiration date to end it.

Can I sell a house with tenants in it?

Yes. Tell the buyer about the lease up front. Check the lease and ask a Delaware attorney how the sale affects the tenant's move-out date.
